body.p: Thank you for the thoughtful assessment of our study. We appreciate your recognition of the novelty and rigor of our approach, as well as the potential implications of our findings for understanding how species-specific regulatory architecture contributes to variation in oxytocin receptor expression and social behavior diversity. We also appreciate your detailed summary of our experimental strategy and findings.

disp-quote.p: Weaknesses:
(1) The expression in the brain and mammary gland (Figure 2) was not quantified, preventing a more objective conclusion that the brain has flexible expression and mammary gland expression is rigid.

body.p: Thank you for raising this important point. In Figure 5 of the manuscript, we showed quantitative analyses of Oxtr expression across different brain regions of Koi lines. In the revised manuscript, we have additionally included quantitative analyses of Oxtr expression in the mammary gland (Supplementary Fig. 5). Together, these analyses support our conclusion that Oxtr expression is more flexible in the brain, whereas its expression in the mammary gland is relatively rigid.

disp-quote.p: (2) In Figure 7, a similar heatmap for the mammary gland is missing.

body.p: Thank you for raising this important point. At the time of our original submission, no Hi-C dataset from mammary gland tissue of any species was available in public repositories. In the manuscript, we therefore analyzed Hi-C datasets from multiple peripheral tissues, which consistently showed TAD architectures that were distinct from those observed in brain-derived tissues. After submission of our manuscript, a human breast-tissue Hi-C dataset was published (Choppavarapu et al., 2025, Cell Reports). Although a mouse mammary-gland Hi-C dataset is still not available, we have now analyzed the Hi-C data generated from normal human mammary gland samples and included these analyses in the revised manuscript (see results and Supplementary Methods). Consistent with the pattern observed across the other peripheral tissues analyzed in our study, the OXTR locus in human mammary tissue is positioned within a pronounced TAD-boundary trough and shows no detectable long-range chromatin interactions (Supplementary Fig. 6A). In contrast, the OXT locus lacks a canonical TAD organization (Supplementary Fig. 6B). Together with our previous analyses of multiple peripheral tissues, these data provide additional support for the distinct 3D genomic organization of the OXTR locus between brain and peripheral tissues, including the mammary gland. They also further support the conclusion that the TAD landscape differs between the Oxtr and Oxt loci.

disp-quote.p: (3) Partner preference in males was not tested.

body.p: Thank you for raising this point. The sex of the animals used for the behavioral experiments was specified in the manuscript (see Results), although we did not explicitly describe our preliminary analyses of partner preference in males. We performed preliminary analyses in both sexes; however, we did not observe robust differences in partner preference among the Koi lines in males. Because reproducible effects were observed in females, we focused our systematic behavioral analyses on females, where the effects were consistent. We have now clarified this point in the revised manuscript (see Results).

disp-quote.p: (4) It is unclear if in the behavioral testing the stimulus animals were the same genotype as the focal female or were wild-types. This could have an impact on the behavioral outcome.

body.p: Thank you for this important clarification. In all behavioral experiments, the stimulus animals were wild-type mice. This design was chosen to minimize potential confounding effects arising from genotype-dependent interactions between stimulus and focal animals. Using standardized wild-type stimulus animals allowed us to more directly assess behavioral differences attributable to the genotype of the focal Koi animals. We have clarified this information in the revised manuscript.

disp-quote.p: Summary:
This is a bold and important study and addresses an important question in the field: how species-specific variation in brain oxytocin receptor expression relates to differences in social behavior.

Tsukamoto et al. generated eight independent transgenic mouse lines (Koi lines) carrying a bacterial artificial chromosome (BAC) encompassing the prairie vole Oxtr locus along with flanking intergenic regions, with the goal of probing the behavioral consequences of species-specific variation in brain Oxtr expression. Across these "volized" lines, the authors claim conserved Oxtr expression in the mammary gland but strikingly divergent patterns of brain expression, none of which fully recapitulate endogenous prairie vole Oxtr distribution, and instead exhibit expression patterns that diverge from both mouse and prairie vole brain Oxtr distribution. Nevertheless, some lines exhibit partial overlap with vole Oxtr expression pattern reported in the literature within specific brain regions, and one line displays partner preference behavior reminiscent of prairie voles. The authors further report line-dependent differences in maternal pup retrieval and crouching behaviors, which they interpret as evidence that variation in brain Oxtr expression can drive variation in social behaviors. Together with analyses of topologically associating domain (TAD) architecture, the authors conclude that brain, but not peripheral- Oxtr expression, is shaped by distal regulatory elements beyond the BAC insert, and propose that such regulatory flexibility underlies evolutionary diversification of social behavior.
Strengths:
A particular strength of the study is the generation of multiple independent transgenic lines, which provides a valuable resource for probing regulatory influences on Oxtr expression.

body.p: Thank you for the careful and thoughtful evaluation of our manuscript. We appreciate your kind recognition of the importance of the question addressed in this study and, in particular, the value of generating multiple independent Koi transgenic lines as a resource for studying regulatory influences on Oxtr expression and mechanism underlying social behavior diversity.

disp-quote.p: Weaknesses:

While the study addresses an important question, I have several methodological and conceptual concerns regarding the study in its current form. Some aspects of the study fall outside my primary area of expertise, and I am therefore not in a position to fully evaluate the technical difficulty or rigor of those components, or to judge whether my suggestions would be feasible to implement. I defer to reviewers with relevant expertise for a more detailed assessment of these aspects.

(1) Each independent Koi line exhibits a distinct brain expression pattern that differs from both wild-type mouse and prairie vole Oxtr expression, complicating the interpretation of the results. The manuscript does not include a direct comparison of brain Oxtr expression patterns in these transgenic lines with those of prairie voles. Instead, expression similarity is inferred primarily from regional localization and compared indirectly with prior literature (Figures 2-5). For those lines that show partial resemblance to prairie vole Oxtr expression patterns, the authors do not assess whether Oxtr-expressing neurons share comparable anatomical projections or transcriptomic identity with prairie vole Oxtr-expressing neurons. Quantification of expression remains largely descriptive, illustrating expression patterns (Figure 2), OXTR protein distribution (Figure 3; images are difficult to evaluate due to low contrast), or Oxtr mRNA levels across selected brain regions in Koi lines, wild-type mice, and mOxtr-/- mice (Figures 4-5), without directly testing similarity to prairie vole expression. In addition, whole-brain expression data are lacking, with analyses restricted to selected sections. While such analyses may be beyond the scope of the present study, these limitations nonetheless complicate interpretation of the central question - namely, whether the observed behavioral phenotypes arise from vole-like Oxtr circuits rather than from distinct, line-specific expression configurations.

body.p: Thank you for this important comment. We agree that a direct comparison with endogenous prairie vole Oxtr expression would facilitate interpretation of the Koi expression patterns. To address this point, we have included representative autoradiographic images of prairie vole brain sections in the revised manuscript (see Supplementary Fig. 4). In addition, a recently published study from Larry’s group using RNAscope provides a detailed reference for the cellular and regional distribution of Oxtr in the prairie vole brain (Kiyoshi et al., 2022). Together, these data provide direct visual references for the spatial distribution of OXTR in key regions, including the PFC, NAc, thalamus, and BLA. Because these datasets were generated using different species and experimental conditions, we have clarified in the figure legends that these comparisons are intended as qualitative assessments of spatial distribution rather than direct quantitative comparisons (see Supplementary Fig. 4 Legend).

Our initial goal was to determine whether prairie vole regulatory elements could reproduce vole-like Oxtr expression patterns in mice. The generation of multiple independent Koi lines revealed that the regulatory elements did not faithfully reproduce a single prairie vole-like expression pattern, but instead generated distinct and partially overlapping expression configurations across lines. This finding led us to a broader question: how can regulatory architecture generate diversity in Oxtr expression patterns, and how does this expression diversity influence social behavior? A major experimental advantage of the Koi system is that all independent Koi lines share the same mouse genetic background and differ primarily in their Oxtr expression configurations. This controlled genetic context allows us to examine the relationship between variation in Oxtr expression and behavioral phenotypes while minimizing the substantial differences in genetic background that exist between mouse and prairie vole. Thus, rather than using the Koi lines as attempts to reproduce the prairie vole brain, we use them as a controlled system to investigate how different spatial configurations of Oxtr expression can contribute to diversity in social behavior. Our findings demonstrate that distinct regulatory configurations can generate diverse Oxtr expression patterns within a common mouse genetic background, and that these different expression configurations are associated with distinct social behavioral outcomes. We have made this point clearer in the revised manuscript.

We also appreciate the reviewer’s suggestion to determine whether Oxtr-expressing neurons in the Koi lines share comparable anatomical projections or transcriptomic identities with Oxtr-expressing neurons in prairie voles. We agree that such analyses would provide important information regarding circuit-level and cellular homology. However, these questions require additional approaches, such as whole-brain mapping of Oxtr expression and projection patterns, single-cell or spatial transcriptomic analyses, and functional manipulation of Oxtr-expressing circuits. These experiments are beyond the scope of the present study and will be important directions for our future investigation.

We specifically examined the PFC, NAc, and BLA because these regions show notable species differences in social behavior-related circuitry and have been implicated in pair-bonding-related behaviors in prairie voles (Amadei et al., 2017; Walum and Young, 2019). The present analyses therefore provide a focused assessment of Oxtr expression in several behaviorally relevant regions. It would be interesting to constitute a whole-brain comparison or establish circuit-level homology between species in the future work.

disp-quote.p: (2) The authors state that Oxtr expression in the mammary gland is similar across all Koi lines and the mOxtr-IRES-Cre knock-in line. However, the images presented in Figure 2 appear to show differences in anatomical detail across lines, and no quantitative analysis is provided to support the claim of equivalence.

body.p: Thank you for this observation. We acknowledge that there are minor differences in staining intensity across mammary gland images in Figure 2. These variations are primarily attributable to technical factors, such as differences in LacZ staining penetration associated with variable lipid content in the mammary fat pad. Importantly, despite these intensity differences, the spatial distribution of LacZ signal is highly consistent across Koi lines, with similar ductal patterns observed throughout the mammary gland. In contrast to the brain—where both the regional distribution and expression levels of Oxtr vary substantially across lines—the mammary gland consistently exhibits robust and widespread expression across all Koi lines. We included quantitative analysis of Oxtr expression in the mammary gland using qRT-PCR (Supplementary Fig5), which shows comparable expression levels across different Koi lines.

disp-quote.p: (3) The conclusion that integration site rather than copy number determines the observed BAC transgene expression patterns (Lines 202-203) is not fully supported by the data. First, the authors did not compare multiple copy numbers at the same genomic insertion site, making it impossible to disentangle copy-number effects from position effects. Second, BAC copy number does not necessarily scale linearly with expression; higher copy numbers can have a repressive effect on gene expression (Garrick et al, Nat Genet, 1998).

body.p: Thank you for this important comment. We agree that the current study cannot fully disentangle the effects of integration site from those of transgene copy number. We also agree that BAC copy number does not necessarily correlate linearly with transgene expression, and that high-copy transgene arrays can lead to transcriptional silencing through mechanisms associated with repressive chromatin states. Importantly, the transgene copy numbers in our Koi lines ranged from 1 to 12 copies, which is substantially lower than the very high-copy arrays associated with transcriptional silencing in the study by Garrick et al. (1998). In that study, the silencing phenotype was observed in mice carrying transgene arrays containing hundreds of copies, and the high-copy arrays were associated with a more condensed and transcriptionally inactive chromatin state. Thus, although we cannot exclude an effect of copy number in our Koi lines, the strong repression associated with very high-copy transgene arrays is unlikely to directly account for the expression variation observed among our relatively low-copy Koi lines. Nevertheless, we acknowledge that the available data do not allow us to conclude that integration site is the sole determinant of the observed expression differences. The current data are consistent with genomic integration site being a major contributor to the variation in BAC transgene expression patterns observed among the Koi lines, while effects of transgene copy number cannot be excluded. We have therefore softened the statement in the revised manuscript (see Results) accordingly.

disp-quote.p: (4) While I am not an expert in TAD analysis, the observed differences in 3D architecture around Oxtr are consistent with a role for long-range regulatory interactions. However, these analyses appear largely descriptive and correlative, and establishing a causal contribution of 3D chromatin organization to Oxtr regulation by distal elements would likely require direct perturbation of TAD boundaries or looping interactions. I recognize that such experiments may be beyond the scope of the present study, but clarifying this limitation in the interpretation would be helpful.

body.p: Thank you for this thoughtful comment. We agree that our analyses of 3D chromatin architecture, while suggestive of a role for long-range regulatory interactions, are inherently correlative in nature. Establishing a causal contribution of TAD organization to distal Oxtr regulation would require a series of experiments including direct perturbation of chromatin structure, through targeted disruption of TAD boundaries or looping interactions using genome engineering approaches. As the reviewer noted, such experiments are technically demanding and beyond the scope of the present study. Accordingly, we have revised the Discussion (see Discussion) to more explicitly acknowledge this limitation. We clarify that our TAD analyses provide a correlative framework supporting the involvement of distal regulatory architecture in shaping brain-specific Oxtr expression, rather than definitive evidence of causality. These findings nonetheless generate testable hypotheses for future studies aimed at directly interrogating the causal role of chromatin architecture in Oxtr regulation.

disp-quote.p: Koi4 line is the only one that replicates the partner preference of prairie voles. This line has low ligand binding in the NAc, unlike the strong expression in the Lac-Z, ISH, and qRT-PCR data. However, ligand binding was strong in the lateral septum and the thalamus. Koi1 and Koi3 also had ligand binding in LS, but not in the thalamus. Taken all together, could this mean that thalamic expression is perhaps what drives partner preference? Given that prairie voles express AvpR1 in the thalamus, and that there is ligand promiscuity between Oxtr and AvpR1a, could the authors speculate whether thalamus vasopressin modulation could play a more important role in partner preference?

body.p: Thank you for raising this insightful point. The Koi-4 line showed robust transgene expression in NAc, as demonstrated by the Lac-Z reporter, RNAscope and qPCR analyses. Notably, strong Oxtr expression in the thalamus was consistently observed across all methods. Recent studies have highlighted important roles for several thalamic nuclei in social memory, social cognition, and the integration of sensory and motivational information (Chen et al., 2024; Rangel, Baldo, & Canteras, 2018; Wolff & Vann, 2019). Given that partner preference likely requires the coordinated engagement of social recognition, social memory, selective attention, arousal, reward processing, and multisensory integration, thalamic Oxtr expression in Koi-4 line may indeed contribute to the behavioral phenotype. Consistent with this possibility, our preliminary chemogenetic experiments suggest that activation of the Oxtr-positive thalamic neurons partially contributed to the parter preference phenotype observed in the Koi-4 line (unpublished data). Therefore, it is possible that vasopressin signaling with thalamic circuits may also contribute to partner preference. While our current data do not allow us to distinguish between vasopressin- and oxytocin- mediated effects, this represents an intriguing hypothesis that warrants future investigation.

disp-quote.p: (1) Lines 262-286 and 289-312: The description of the statistical analyses in the Results section is overly detailed and sometimes difficult to follow. The authors could improve clarity by leading with the main behavioral findings and reserving the full statistical reporting for the Methods section.

body.p: Thank you for your helpful comment. We agree that presenting the main behavioral findings before the detailed statistical results improves the clarity and readability of the Results section. We have therefore revised the descriptions of the Partner Preference Test (see Results) and Pup Retrieval Test (see Results) to lead with the main behavioral findings, followed by the statistical results supporting those findings. We have retained the relevant test statistics, degrees of freedom, exact p-values, and post hoc comparisons for the key analyses in the Results section, while the statistical procedures and analytical approaches are described in detail in the Methods section (see Materials and Methods). These revisions make the main biological findings more readily apparent while maintaining complete statistical reporting.

disp-quote.p: (2) The authors report quantitative differences in pup retrieval latency and crouching behavior in virgin females between two Koi lines with distinct Oxtr expression patterns. However, it is unclear how these behavioral differences relate to prairie vole phenotypes. Specifically, do prairie vole virgin females differ from mice in pup retrieval latency or crouching duration, and if so, which of the Koi lines more closely resemble vole behavior? Direct behavioral comparisons with prairie voles would have helped address this question. This comparison is important given the stated motivation for these experiments - that Oxtr expression in certain brain regions resembles vole patterns (albeit across separate lines) and is postulated to underlie vole-typical social behaviors. As currently presented, the manuscript appears to pivot from testing vole-relevant behaviors to testing whether different Oxtr expression patterns in mice produce different maternal behaviors, without clearly establishing how these behaviors map onto vole-specific traits. If these phenotypes are known to differ between species, a brief discussion of the relevant literature would help contextualize the findings.

body.p: Thank you for raising this important point. We agree that direct comparisons of parental behaviors between prairie voles and mice would be informative for determining whether the Koi phenotypes resemble species-specific vole traits. However, such a comparison was not the primary objective of our experiments.

Our initial goal was to determine whether the prairie vole Oxtr locus and its surrounding regulatory elements could reproduce vole-like Oxtr expression patterns in mice. The distinct and partially overlapping expression configurations observed across independent Koi lines led us to a broader question: how does variation in Oxtr regulatory architecture generate diversity in expression patterns and, consequently, social behaviors? Accordingly, the pup retrieval and crouching assays were designed to test whether distinct pvOXTR expression configurations are associated with quantitative differences in parental behavior, rather than to determine which Koi line most closely resembles a prairie vole phenotype. We have made this point clearer in the revised manuscript (see Introduction).

disp-quote.p: (3) The partner preference test is a well-established assay; however, a direct comparison of behavioral phenotypes obtained in this assay between prairie voles and the Koi lines would be an important control. Such a comparison would help establish whether the behavioral patterns observed in the Koi lines meaningfully approximate prairie vole partner preference under identical experimental conditions.

body.p: Thank you for this important suggestion. We agree that a direct comparison with prairie voles under identical experimental conditions would be valuable for determining whether the behavioral phenotypes of the Koi lines quantitatively approximate prairie vole partner preference. However, the primary purpose of the PPT in this study was not to establish a prairie vole-like behavioral phenotype in a particular Koi line, but to determine whether distinct pvOXTR expression configurations are associated with differences in social preference within the same mouse genetic background.

Importantly, we do not intend to claim that Koi-2 or Koi-4 represents a behavioral phenocopy of prairie voles. Rather, our aim was to test whether divergent OXTR regulatory and expression configurations can generate divergent social behaviors. The contrasting partner versus stranger preferences observed in Koi-2 and Koi-4 provide evidence consistent with this possibility. We have clarified this rationale in the revised manuscript (see Introduction).

disp-quote.p: (4) A recent study reported that prairie voles lacking oxytocin receptors, generated via CRISPR-mediated deletion, nonetheless exhibit largely intact social attachment behaviors, including pair bonding, parental care, and successful nursing to weaning (Brendenzen et al., Neuron, 2023). How do the authors interpret their findings in light of this study (i.e., intact social behavior in Oxtr knockout voles)? One plausible explanation is that constitutive deletion during development, as shown in Brendenzen et al., may engage compensatory or redundant pathways that restore behavior, while differences in Oxtr expression nonetheless contribute to the social variation observed between prairie voles and mice. A brief discussion of this possibility would help situate the present results within the broader literature in the field.

body.p: Thank you for raising this important point. We agree that the findings of Berendzen et al. are highly relevant to the interpretation of our results. The apparent discrepancy may reflect an important difference between constitutive loss of OXTR signaling and variation in the spatial distribution of OXTR expression. In the CRISPR-mediated Oxtr knockout voles, OXTR signaling is absent from development onward, yet these animals retain pair bonding and parental behaviors (Berendzen et al., 2023). One possibility is that the absence of OXTR signaling during development allows compensatory or redundant mechanisms to develop. Consistent with this interpretation, Larry Young proposed that the timing of OXTR loss may be critical, with neural circuits potentially becoming dependent on oxytocin signaling through developmental exposure to the hormone.

Our Koi system provides a complementary approach. Rather than eliminating OXTR signaling, the Koi lines preserve pvOXTR expression while generating distinct spatial expression patterns within the same mouse genetic background. We found that these divergent pvOXTR expression patterns were associated with distinct social behavioral phenotypes across the Koi lines. The divergent social phenotypes observed across these lines suggest that variation in the spatial organization of OXTR expression, rather than simply the presence or absence of OXTR signaling, may contribute to behavioral diversity. Thus, the intact social behaviors of constitutive Oxtr knockout voles do not exclude a role for OXTR expression patterns in shaping behavioral variation. We have added a discussion of this possibility and of the findings of Brendenzen et al. (2023) to the revised manuscript (see Discussion).

disp-quote.p: Should you choose to revise your manuscript, if you have not already done so, please include full statistical reporting including exact p-values wherever possible alongside the summary statistics (test statistic and df) and, where appropriate, 95% confidence intervals. These should be reported for all key questions and not only when the p-value is less than 0.05 in the main manuscript.

body.p: Thank you for this guidance. We had reported the test statistics, degrees of freedom, and exact p-values for the statistical analyses in the original manuscript, including both significant and nonsignificant results. Nevertheless, we carefully reviewed the statistical reporting throughout the manuscript and revised the Results section to ensure that the relevant test statistics, degrees of freedom, and exact p-values are consistently reported alongside the corresponding findings. We also reorganized the descriptions of the behavioral results to present the main findings more clearly before the detailed statistical results, as suggested by Reviewer #2.
